# Acid-degradable lipid nanoparticles enhance the delivery of mRNA

**Authors:** Sheng Zhao; Kewa Gao; Hesong Han; Michael Stenzel; Boyan Yin; Hengyue Song; Atip Lawanprasert; Josefine Eilsø Nielsen; Rohit Sharma; Opeyemi H. Arogundade; Sopida Pimcharoen; Yu-Ju Chen; Abhik Paul; Jan Tuma; Michael G. Collins; Yofiel Wyle; Matileen Grace Cranick; Benjamin W. Burgstone; Barbara S. Perez; Annelise E. Barron; Andrew M. Smith; Hye Young Lee; Aijun Wang; Niren Murthy

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Bioengineering and Innovative Genomics Institute, University of California, Berkeley, CA, USA. | 2Department of Surgery, Department of Biomedical Engineering and Institute for Pediatric Regenerative Medicine/Shriners Children’s, University of California, Davis, Sacramento, CA, USA. | 3Department of Science and Environment, Roskilde University, Roskilde, Denmark. | 4Department of Bioengineering, School of Medicine, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA. | 5Department of Bioengineering and Cancer Center at Illinois, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL, USA. | 6Department of Cellular and Integrative Physiology, University of Texas, Health Science Center at San Antonio, San Antonio, TX, USA. | 7Department of Pathophysiology, Faculty of Medicine in Pilsen, Charles University, Plzen, Czech Republic. | 8These authors contributed equally: Sheng Zhao, Kewa Gao, Hesong Han.

## Abstract

Lipid nanoparticle (LNP)–mRNA complexes are transforming medicine. However, the medical applications of LNPs are limited by their low endosomal disruption rates, high toxicity and long tissue persistence times. LNPs that rapidly hydrolyse in endosomes (RD-LNPs) could solve the problems limiting LNP-based therapeutics and dramatically expand their applications but have been challenging to synthesize. Here we present an acid-degradable linker termed ‘azido-acetal’ that hydrolyses in endosomes within minutes and enables the production of RD-LNPs. Acid-degradable lipids composed of polyethylene glycol lipids, anionic lipids and cationic lipids were synthesized with the azido-acetal linker and used to generate RD-LNPs, which significantly improved the performance of LNP–mRNA complexes in vitro and in vivo. Collectively, RD-LNPs delivered mRNA more efficiently to the liver, lung, spleen and brains of mice and to haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells in vitro than conventional LNPs. These experiments demonstrate that engineering LNP hydrolysis rates in vivo has great potential for expanding the medical applications of LNPs.

Lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-based delivery vectors are revolutionizing medicine. However, LNP–mRNA complexes have limitations that prevent them from serving as a platform for new therapeutics. For example, LNP–mRNA complexes deliver only 1–4% of their mRNA cargo into the cytoplasm1. The low endosomal disruption rate of LNPs restricts their medical applications because large amounts of mRNA need to be delivered into cells to generate therapeutic quantities of proteins. The liver is the only organ that internalizes LNPs robustly enough to compensate for the low endosomal disruption rates of LNPs, and developing LNP–mRNA complexes for non-liver diseases will require engineering LNPs to efficiently disrupt endosomes2. In addition, LNPs exhibit high levels of toxicity, due to their cationic and ionizable lipids, and also persist in tissues for days to weeks3. These issues prevent LNP–mRNA complexes from being chronically administered and limits their dose. Collectively, the low endosomal disruption rate, toxicity and tissue persistence of LNP–mRNA complexes prevent them from treating numerous diseases, and strategies for improving their performance are needed. LNPs that degrade in endosomes within 30 min (termed RD-LNPs) have the potential to address several of the limitations of conventional LNPs. In particular, endosomal trafficking to lysosomes occurs within 30–60 min, and RD-LNPs will degrade in endosomes before fusion with lysosomes occurs. The rapid hydrolysis of the RD-LNPs should enable them to trigger endosomal disruption and release endocytosed mRNA into the cytoplasm before mRNA degradation in the lysosomes occurs4. In addition, RD-LNPs should get cleared from cells faster than conventional LNPs, and this should lower their toxicity and accumulation within tissues.

Acid-degradable lipids (ADLs) have great potential for generating RD-LNPs, given the pH gradient between the endosome and the blood. For example, early endosomes have a pH of 6.0, and late endosomes have a pH of 5.0, whereas the blood is at pH 7.4. There is consequently great interest in developing ADLs and using them to formulate RD-LNPs5,6. ADLs have been synthesized with linkages based on vinyl ethers7, orthoesters8, ketals9, acetals2,10,11 and hydrazones12 and have been incorporated into liposomes, cationic liposomes and LNPs and have generated promising results. However, existing ADLs degrade on the timescale of days at pH 6.0–6.8 and on the timescale of hours at pH 5.0–6.0 and are consequently trafficked to lysosomes, where they are degraded. Developing ADLs that rapidly hydrolyse at pH 6.0 has been challenging. The hydrolysis rate of conventional acid-degradable linkers is proportional to the hydronium ion concentration13, and consequently, linkers that rapidly hydrolyse at pHs 6.0–6.8 are also unstable at pH 7.4 and difficult to use.

In this Article, we present an acid-degradable linker termed ‘azido-acetal’ that solves the problems associated with developing linkers that rapidly degrade in endosomes and hydrolyses in endosomes within minutes but is stable at pH 7.4 for 21 days. The azido-acetal linker is composed of a benzaldehyde acetal that has an azido in its para position and hydrolyses via a two-step mechanism that requires reduction followed by acid hydrolysis (Fig. 1). This two-step hydrolysis mechanism allows the azido-acetal to have a unique combination of stability and rapid hydrolysis at mildly acidic pHs. The azido-acetal has a slow hydrolysis rate due to the weak electron-withdrawing character of the azido (Hammett sigma value 0.1)14, enabling the synthesis of ADLs in high yields and their incorporation into LNPs in aqueous environments. However, before administration, the azido-acetal is reduced to an amine via the addition of thiols. This reduction accelerates the azido-acetal’s hydrolysis rate because of the strong electron-donating character of the amine (Hammett sigma value −0.66)14,15.

We demonstrate here that the azido-acetal linker can be used as a platform for generating RD-LNPs and further demonstrate that RD-LNPs are superior to traditional LNPs with regard to delivering mRNA to the liver, lung, spleen and brains of mice and to haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) in vitro. For example, RD-LNPs designed to deliver mRNA to the lungs rescued mice from acute lung injury via the delivery of IL-22 mRNA, whereas traditional LNPs could not. In addition, RD-LNPs that contained high levels of PEGylation efficiently delivered Cas9 mRNA and guide RNA (gRNA) to brain tissue and edited five times the number of brain cells as traditional LNPs. Collectively, these studies demonstrate that engineering LNP hydrolysis rates in vivo has great potential for expanding the medical applications of LNPs.

## The azido-acetal hydrolyses rapidly at pH 6.0 after reduction

We synthesized the model azido-acetal 4 and measured its acid-catalysed hydrolysis rate before and after reduction (see Supplementary Figs. 3-1 and 3-2 for details). Supplementary Table 1 demonstrates that the reduction of an azido-acetal dramatically increases its hydrolysis rate. For example, compound 4 experienced under 1% hydrolysis after 3 h at pH 7.4 and had a predicted hydrolysis half-life of 21 days at pH 7.4 at 37 °C. However, after reduction, the hydrolysis half-life of 4 was accelerated by a factor of 255, and the reduced 4 had a hydrolysis half-life of 2 h at pH 7.4 and 14.8 min at pH 6.0. At pH 7.4, 4 is more stable than mRNA and has a hydrolysis half-life similar to the ester linkages found in LNP-forming lipids and should have the stability needed for formulating and storing LNPs. In addition, the reduced azido-acetal hydrolyses with t½ < 30 min at pH 6.0 and has the hydrolysis kinetics needed to degrade in endosomes before trafficking to lysosomes occurs4.

## Acid-degradable PEG lipids enhance the delivery of mRNA

We used the azido-acetal to synthesize the acid-degradable polyethylene glycol (PEG) lipid 1 and made LNPs with 1, termed ADP-LNPs (see Supplementary Table 2 for hydrolysis half-life of 1). The morphology and size of ADP-LNPs were investigated via dynamic light scattering (DLS), small angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) and cryogenic transmission electron microscopy (cryo-TEM) (see Supplementary Figs. 6-3, 6-4 and 6-5 for details). We selected the PEG lipid as an initial lipid to investigate because of its important role in determining the biophysical and biological properties of an LNP. For example, the PEG lipid can increase the circulation time of an LNP16 and enhance its diffusion through tissue17,18. The PEG lipid can also lower the endosomal disruption rate of an LNP and induce the formation of anti-PEG antibodies. LNPs used in clinical products are now made with 0.5–1.5 mol% of the PEG lipid. This range of PEG lipid generates LNPs with an optimal size for current clinical applications, which are focused on liver delivery after an intravenous injection and vaccine development. LNPs have numerous applications beyond liver delivery and vaccine development, such as delivery via inhalation or intracranial injections. For these other applications, LNPs with higher amounts of PEG may be beneficial. Engineering the PEG lipid to rapidly hydrolyse in endosomes has the potential to generate LNPs with high levels of PEGylation18 that also transfect cells efficiently7,19–23, and this may enable new medical applications of LNPs.

We investigated if LNPs made with high levels of 1 could transfect HEK 293T cells and compared their transfection ability against LNPs made with a non-degradable PEG2k–cholesterol conjugate (termed NDP-LNPs) (see Fig. 2a and Supplementary Fig. 6-1 for details). The results are shown in Fig. 2b and demonstrate that ADP-LNPs containing 10 and 20 mol% of 1 were efficient at transfecting HEK 293T cells and even had moderate efficiency at 40 mol% of 1. In contrast, NDP-LNPs containing 20 mol% of PEG lipid were ineffective at transfecting cells. The total amount of protein generated from cells treated with ADP-LNPs and NDP-LNPs containing luciferase mRNA was investigated to determine if rapid hydrolysis of the PEG lipid increases mRNA delivery efficiency. Figure 2c demonstrates that cells treated with ADP-LNP/luciferase mRNA had substantially more luciferase activity than NDP-LNPs. The ability of ADP-LNPs to escape endosomes was also investigated via fluorescent microscopy using the Galectin-8 reporter cell line24. The results demonstrated that ADP-LNPs can escape endosomes more efficiently than NDP-LNPs (Supplementary Figs. 10-7 and 10-8). ADP-LNPs also retained their transfection efficiency after storing at −80 °C or 4 °C for 60 days (Supplementary Fig. 7-5). Collectively, these results demonstrate that the acid degradability of ADP-LNPs plays an essential role in enabling efficient mRNA delivery and that they have the stability needed for product development.

We investigated if ADP-LNPs containing green fluorescent protein (GFP) mRNA could transfect HSPCs and compared their efficacy against standard LNPs (Std-LNPs) and electroporation (EP). We selected HSPCs as a testbed for the ADP-LNPs because of the great need for new HSPC transfection reagents that are efficient and have low toxicity25–28. The results showed that ADP-LNPs achieved 90% transfection of HSPCs while maintaining 60% cell viability at a dose of 10 μg ml−1 of mRNA (Fig. 2d). In contrast, Std-LNPs caused high levels of toxicity to HSPCs and were only able to transfect about 50% of the HSPCs owing to dose-limiting toxicity. We anticipate that the lower toxicity of the ADP-LNPs is due to their high levels of PEGylation, which should shield their positive charges from the cell membrane of HSPC29. In addition, we compared the transfection efficacy of ADP-LNPs with EP. HSPCs electroporated with enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP) mRNA had a transfection rate of 82%, but their cell viability was only 35% (Fig. 2d). We also investigated if ADP-LNPs could deliver Cas9 mRNA and gRNA to HSPCs and edit HSPCs. Cas9 mRNA and gRNA targeting the AAVS1 gene were co-delivered to HSPCs with ADP-LNPs and subsequently analysed for gene editing. Figure 2e demonstrates that ADP-LNPs generated 30% indels in HSPCs and suggests they have potential as a transfection reagent for generating HSPC-based cell therapy products.

We next investigated the ability of ADP-LNPs to deliver mRNA to mice and compared their efficacy against LNPs that contained dimyristoyl glycerol-PEG (Std-LNPs; Supplementary Table 10) or NDP-LNPs. We first performed a pharmacokinetic study with fluorescently labelled ADP-LNPs to determine if the dense PEGylation of the ADP-LNPs increased their circulation half-life compared with Std-LNPs30,31. Supplementary Fig. 9-3 demonstrates that the circulation half-life of the ADP-LNPs was 47 min, which was longer than Std-LNPs (t½ = 6 min) and the commonly used Onpattro formulation containing EGFP mRNA (t½ = 15 min (ref. 31); Supplementary Table 11). The organ tropism of ADP-LNPs was investigated using ADP-LNPs containing luciferase mRNA. Ex vivo imaging (Supplementary Fig. 9-2) of Ai9 mice treated with ADP-LNPs demonstrated that they primarily transfected the liver and spleen and delivered nine and four times more luciferase mRNA to the liver and spleen than NDP-LNPs (Fig. 2f). ADP-LNPs were also well tolerated after an intravenous injection at a dose of 20 μg mRNA and had an immunogenic toxicity profile similar to Std-LNPs (Supplementary Fig. 7-4).

Next, we performed experiments to determine the in vivo cell tropism of ADP-LNPs containing Cre mRNA using Ai9 mice. Ai9 mice were injected with ADP-LNPs, and after 2 weeks, the mice were killed and analysed. The results revealed that ADP-LNPs transfected approximately 90% of the cells in the liver (Fig. 2g,h) and transfected major liver cell types, such as hepatocytes, macrophages and endothelial cells (Supplementary Figs. 9–10a). In addition, ADP-LNPs also transfected 25% of the cells in the spleen (Fig. 2g,h) and specifically targeted macrophages, which are the target of numerous immuno-engineering-based therapeutics (Supplementary Figs. 9–10a).

## LNPs made with acid-degradable PEG lipids transfect brain tissue efficiently

Finally, we investigated if the ADP-LNPs containing Cre mRNA could efficiently transfect brain tissue after an intracranial injection using the Ai9 mouse model32,33. The extracellular matrix of the brain is ‘sticky’ and prevents nanoparticles from transfecting brain tissue efficiently after an intracranial injection, due to their limited diffusion. PEGylation can increase the diffusion of nanoparticles in brain tissues1, and we therefore hypothesized that ADP-LNPs with 10% PEG would transfect brain tissue more efficiently than conventional LNPs, which contain about 1.5 mol% PEG. LNP–mRNA complexes were injected into the hippocampus and striatum, and their transfection efficiency was evaluated by analysing histology sections of the brain for tdTomato-positive cells. ADP-LNPs transfected the striatum and hippocampus after an intracranial injection with high efficiency and transfected approximately 30% of the cells in the striatum and hippocampus (Supplementary Figs. 9-4 and 9-5). Furthermore, ADP-LNPs diffused from the injection site in both the striatum and hippocampus and transfected millimetres of tissue.

We performed additional experiments to investigate if ADP-LNPs could deliver Cas9 mRNA and gRNA into brain tissue, using the Ai9 mouse model, and compared their delivery efficiency against Std-LNPs, which contained about 1.5% PEG. Cas9 mRNA and gRNA were selected as mRNA cargo because of the great therapeutic potential of gene editing in the brain. ADP-LNPs were injected into the hippocampus, and after 21 days, gene editing in the brain was analysed by counting the tdTomato-positive cells. Figure 2i,j demonstrates that ADP-LNPs were significantly better at transfecting brain tissue with Cas9 mRNA and gRNA than Std-LNPs and transfected five times the number of cells in the brain as Std-LNPs (spatial distribution of transfected cells in the brain is shown in Supplementary Fig. 9-6). Collectively, the experiments with ADP-LNPs demonstrate they can deliver mRNA efficiently to HSPCs and brain tissue and outperform traditional methods owing to their unique combination of dense PEGylation and rapid hydrolysis in endosomes.

## LNPs containing acid-degradable anionic lipids disrupt endosomes

The versatility and chemical stability of the azido-acetal linker allowed us to develop other new classes of ADLs. Anionic lipids were selected as the second lipid for engineering acid-catalysed hydrolysis. LNPs that contain an anionic lipid have generated great interest because of their ability to target the spleen and mitigate the toxicity of LNPs by increasing their negative charge density34,35. However, LNPs with a negative charge density have low transfection efficiency because a positive surface charge density is required to trigger efficient cell uptake and endosomal disruption36. To address this, we synthesized the anionic lipid 2, which contains three carboxylic acids connected to cholesterol via the azido-acetal linker. LNPs formulated with a high mole ratio of 2 (termed ADA-LNPs) are expected to possess a negative surface charge density and consequently target the spleen. ADA-LNPs are also engineered to trigger endosomal disruption. The hydrolysis of 2 in endosomes is anticipated to increase the osmolarity of the endosome by >33 mM (see Supplementary Section 11 for calculation), which would increase the osmolarity of the endosome by more than 10% and induce osmotic destabilization of the endosome37. In addition, the charge density of the ADA-LNPs will also become more positive in endosomes, and this should facilitate their fusion with the anionic lipids in the endosomal membrane (Fig. 3a).

The transfection ability of LNPs made with 2 (ADA-LNPs) was compared against LNPs made with the non-degradable anionic lipids C-18 phosphatidic acid (18PA, termed NDA1-LNPs) and compound 6 (termed NDA2-LNPs). In addition, the size and morphology of ADA-LNPs were also investigated via DLS, SAXS and cryo-TEM (see Supplementary Figs. 6-3b, 6-4b and 6-5b for details). The ADA-LNPs were substantially better at transfecting HEK 293T cells than NDA1-LNPs. For example, ADA-LNPs transfected >80% of cells with EGFP mRNA, whereas NDA1-LNPs transfected only 50% of cells at maximum (Fig. 3b). In addition, ADA-LNPs were also able to deliver luciferase mRNA to HEK 293T cells more efficiently than NDA1-LNPs and generated approximately 45–145 times higher levels of luciferase expression in cells than NDA1-LNPs (Fig. 3c). In addition, cells treated with ADA-LNPs containing IL-22 mRNA generated 8–13 times more IL-22 protein in their supernatants than NDA1-LNPs (Fig. 3d).

We performed fluorescent microscopy experiments with ADA-LNPs containing quantum dot–DNA conjugates to determine if the rapid hydrolysis of 2 enhanced endosomal disruption. Fluorescent microscopy of quantum dots can quantify endosomal disruption rates by measurement of their intracellular diffusion coefficients and trajectories38. Figure 3e demonstrates that ADA-LNPs rapidly induced endosomal release of the quantum dot–DNA conjugates and caused approximately 60% of the endocytosed quantum dots to be released from the endosome. In contrast, NDA1-LNPs and Std-LNPs largely remained in endosomes, and only 20% of their endocytosed quantum dots were released from the endosome. The ability of ADA-LNPs to escape endosomes was further investigated with the Galectin-8 reporter cell line24. Supplementary Fig. 10-8 verifies the quantum dot results with ADA-LNPs and demonstrates that ADA-LNPs were able to permeabilize endosomes and disrupt them efficiently. These results demonstrate that RD-LNPs can efficiently trigger endosomal disruption and also enhance the mRNA delivery efficiency of anionic LNPs.

We performed experiments to investigate the ability of ADA-LNPs to deliver mRNA in vivo using luciferase mRNA and Cre mRNA. Mice were injected with ADA-LNPs encapsulating luciferase mRNA and analysed through whole-body and ex vivo imaging (Supplementary Figs. 9-1 and 9-2). Figure 3f demonstrates that ADA-LNPs generated luciferase activity in the spleen that was approximately eight times higher than NDA1-LNPs or NDA2-LNPs. The cell tropism and transfection efficiency of ADA-LNPs were assessed by delivering Cre mRNA to Ai9 mice. ADA-LNPs transfected 32% of the cells in the spleen and 45% of the cells in the liver (Fig. 3g). Histological analysis (Fig. 3h,i) indicated that ADA-LNPs primarily transfected macrophages in the spleen, amounting to approximately 25% of the macrophages. In addition, ADA-LNPs also transfected approximately 5% of the B cells in the spleen, while hepatocytes were the predominant cell type transfected in the liver. These experiments demonstrate the potential of ADA-LNPs as therapeutics for treating various immune disorders and demonstrate that the azido-acetal linker can serve as a platform for developing new ADLs for mRNA delivery.

## LNPs containing acid-degradable cationic lipids efficiently transfect lung tissue

Finally, we investigated if engineering rapid hydrolysis in the endosome could improve the transfection efficiency of cationic lipids (Fig. 4a). LNPs containing cationic lipids transfect lung tissue efficiently and have great potential as a platform for generating lung therapeutics18,35,39–41. However, current cationic lipids have several problems that limit their clinical applications. For example, cationic lipids such as 1,2-dioleoyl-3-trimethylammonium propane (DOTAP) and didodecyldimethylammonium bromide (DDAB) degrade slowly in cells and generate membrane-impermeable cations10. Consequently, treating patients with multiple doses of cationic lipids is challenging because of their tissue accumulation. In addition, cationic lipids generate toxicity because of their positive charges and their persistence within cells42. There are consequently no Food and Drug Administration-approved LNP formulations that contain cationic lipids.

The acid-degradable cationic lipid 3 has the potential to address several problems associated with cationic lipids. 3 hydrolyses in cells orders of magnitude faster than conventional cationic lipids and should therefore be amenable to repeat dosing. In addition, 3 degrades into biocompatible or membrane-permeable products and should generate LNPs (termed ADC-LNPs) with mitigated toxicity. In particular, 3 degrades into the essential metabolite choline, the natural lipid cholesterol and the non-toxic compound 4-amino benzaldehyde43,44. The rapid hydrolysis of 3 in endosomes may also enhance the transfection efficiency of LNPs by stimulating endosomal disruption via the colloid osmotic effect37 and by triggering de-complexation of the mRNA in the endosome.

The mRNA transfection efficiency of ADC-LNPs was compared against LNPs made with DOTAP (NDC-LNPs) in HEK 293T cells using LNPs that encapsulated luciferase mRNA or IL-22 mRNA. In addition, the size and morphology of ADC-LNPs were also investigated via DLS, SAXS and cryo-TEM (see Supplementary Figs. 6-3c, 6-4c and 6-5c for details). Figure 4c,d demonstrates that LNPs made with 3 can deliver mRNA to HEK 293T cells better than NDC-LNPs. ADC-LNPs produced approximately four times the luciferase signal and two times more IL-22 protein than NDC-LNPs. We also investigated the ability of ADC-LNPs to escape endosomes via fluorescent microscopy using the Galectin-8 reporter cell line. Supplementary Fig. 10-8 demonstrates that ADC-LNPs can permeabilize endosomes and induce endosomal escape. The azido-acetal linker can therefore generate diverse classes of lipids and should be able to engineer acid sensitivity in a wide range of new lipid-based compounds.

We investigated if ADC-LNPs could transfect human HSPCs and compared their efficacy against Std-LNPs. Figure 4e demonstrates that ADC-LNPs containing 5 or 10 mol% of 3 and GFP mRNA transfected 70% of HSPCs and caused minimal toxicity. In contrast, as shown in Fig. 2d and Supplementary Fig. 7-2, Std-LNPs only generated 50% transfection and caused >95% toxicity. In addition, ADC-LNPs were also able to deliver Cas9 mRNA and gRNA to HSPCs and generated 48% indels in the AAVS1 gene, demonstrating they have potential as a platform for developing new cell-based therapies (Fig. 4f).

Mouse experiments were performed with ADC-LNPs containing 40 mol% of 3 and luciferase mRNA to determine if they could transfect lung tissue. ADC-LNPs generated a lung signal close to 109 photons s−1 cm−2 sr−1 (Fig. 4g). In contrast NDC-LNPs containing 40 mol% of DOTAP primarily transfected the spleen. A Cre mRNA delivery experiment using Ai9 mice was performed to determine the cell tropism of ADC-LNPs. ADC-LNPs transfected approximately 50% of the cells in the lung after a single injection (Fig. 4h), and histological analysis demonstrated that the transfected cells were predominantly in the smaller airways and were localized around the alveolus. In the alveolar region, the ADC-LNP transfection rates were >70% (Fig. 4i,j), and both epithelial cells and endothelial cells were efficiently transfected. A variety of diseases, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, acute lung injury and lung cancer, originate from pathologies in endothelial and epithelial cells located in the alveolus45. ADC-LNPs, therefore, have the potential to serve as a platform for developing new lung therapeutics.

We used ADC-LNPs to develop a potential therapeutic for acute lung injury based on delivering IL-22 mRNA to the lung. IL-22 can treat a variety of lung inflammatory diseases46–48 but has been challenging to develop because of its high toxicity and short circulation half-life (under 2 h)49. Lung-targeted LNPs have the potential to localize IL-22 in the lung and thereby generate a higher therapeutic window than soluble IL-22 protein, which has no targeting ability. IL-22 mRNA was encapsulated into ADC-LNPs, and their ability to produce therapeutic concentrations of IL-22 protein in the blood via lung transfection was investigated. Figure 4k shows that ADC-LNPs generated a peak IL-22 concentration of 120 ng ml−1 after 4 h and maintained a therapeutic concentration in the blood for >24 h with a single injection. Based on this, we investigated if ADC-LNPs containing IL-22 mRNA could rescue mice from acute lung injury and compared their therapeutic efficacy against Std-LNPs that primarily transfect the liver. Mice were given intravenous injections of ADC-LNPs or control LNPs and challenged with an intratracheal injection of lipopolysaccharide (LPS). After being killed, the protein content in their bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) was measured. Figure 4l demonstrates that ADC-LNPs significantly reduced the protein content in the BALF in comparison with LPS-treated mice, whereas Std-LNPs were unable to do so. ADC-LNPs containing cytokine mRNA have significant benefits over Std-LNPs and should enable the development of new lung therapeutics. Finally, these experiments further validate the azido-acetal linker as a platform for developing RD-LNPs and new acid-degradable materials.

Although the RD-LNPs were able to improve the transfection efficiency of LNPs in multiple cases, they have limitations. For example, RD-LNPs require mixing with a reducing agent before administration, and this may cause challenges with clinical translation. The complications caused by the reducing agent can potentially be mitigated by reducing the RD-LNPs with compounds that have a reducing power similar to dithiothreitol (DTT), which have been ingested by people, such as α-lipoic acid. In addition, the RD-LNPs contain a high amount of cholesterol because 1, 2 and 3 contain cholesterol. The cumulative cholesterol content in the RD-LNPs may be close to the saturation point of cholesterol and may even exceed it at high concentrations of 1, 2 and 3. Future generations of RD-LNPs may need to replace the cholesterol groups in 1, 2 and 3 with other hydrophobic groups that have a lower tendency to phase separate than cholesterol. Finally, ADP-LNPs contain large amounts of the PEG lipid, and some formulations contained as much as 40 mol% PEG lipid. These high concentrations of the PEG lipid may trigger phase separation, which may limit the amount of PEG lipid that can be introduced into the RD-LNPs.

## Conclusions

In this Article, we present a new class of LNPs that rapidly hydrolyse in endosomes, termed RD-LNPs, which were synthesized using the azido-acetal linker. RD-LNPs enhanced the delivery of mRNA across a variety of cell types and organs and outperformed traditional LNPs in multiple organs. Collectively, the experiments presented here demonstrate that engineering LNP hydrolysis rates in vivo has great potential for expanding the medical applications of LNPs.
